name: Mercury
desc: The smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. With almost no atmosphere to trap heat, its surface swings between scorching days and freezing nights.
fact: A single solar day on Mercury (sunrise to sunrise) lasts about 176 Earth days — two of its years.

name: Venus
desc: Similar in size to Earth, but wrapped in a crushing CO₂ atmosphere about 92 times denser than ours. A runaway greenhouse effect makes it the hottest planet.
fact: Venus spins backwards (retrograde) — on Venus the Sun rises in the west.

name: Earth
desc: Our home — the only world known to host life, with liquid water covering about 71% of its surface and a protective magnetic field.
fact: Earth is the densest planet in the Solar System (5.51 g/cm³).

name: Mars
desc: The Red Planet owes its colour to iron oxide dust. It hosts Olympus Mons, the tallest volcano in the Solar System, and Valles Marineris, a canyon as long as the USA.
fact: NASA rovers Curiosity and Perseverance are still exploring Mars today.

name: Jupiter
desc: The largest planet — more than twice as massive as all the others combined. Its Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth that has raged for centuries.
fact: Jupiter spins faster than any other planet: a day lasts under 10 hours.

name: Saturn
desc: Famous for its spectacular rings of ice and rock. Saturn is the least dense planet — on average less dense than water.
fact: Saturn has the most known moons of any planet; its moon Titan has lakes of liquid methane.

name: Uranus
desc: An ice giant tipped on its side, probably after an ancient collision. Methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light, giving it a pale cyan colour.
fact: Because of its 98° tilt, each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, then 42 years of darkness.

name: Neptune
desc: The most distant planet, discovered in 1846 by mathematics before anyone saw it. It has the fastest winds in the Solar System — over 2,000 km/h.
fact: Neptune has completed only about one orbit since it was discovered (it finished its first in 2011).

name: Sun
desc: A 4.6-billion-year-old star holding 99.86% of the Solar System’s mass. Nuclear fusion in its core turns about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium every second.
fact: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes 20 seconds to reach Earth.

name: Moon
desc: Earth’s only natural satellite, probably formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth. Its gravity drives our ocean tides.
fact: The Moon is tidally locked — we always see the same side. It drifts about 3.8 cm farther from Earth each year.

name: Ceres
desc: The largest object in the asteroid belt and the first asteroid ever found (Giuseppe Piazzi, 1801). NASA’s Dawn spacecraft orbited it from 2015 to 2018 — the first mission to orbit a dwarf planet.
fact: The bright spots in Occator crater are salt deposits left behind by briny water that seeped up from below the surface.

name: Pluto
desc: Discovered by Clyde Tombaugh in 1930 and reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006. NASA’s New Horizons flew past in July 2015 and revealed mountains of water ice and a vast heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice.
fact: Pluto and its moon Charon are tidally locked to each other — Charon hangs motionless in the same spot of Pluto’s sky.

name: Eris
desc: Almost exactly Pluto’s size but about 27% more massive. Its discovery in 2005 forced astronomers to define what a planet is — and led to Pluto’s reclassification in 2006.
fact: Eris is near the far end of its tilted, stretched orbit right now — sunlight takes over 13 hours to reach it.

name: Haumea
desc: Stretched into an egg shape by its extremely fast spin — a day lasts under four hours. It has two moons and, surprisingly, a thin ring discovered in 2017.
fact: Haumea is one of the fastest-rotating large objects known in the Solar System.

name: Makemake
desc: A reddish-brown world coated in frozen methane, discovered in March 2005 shortly after Easter — so it was named after the creator god of the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island.
fact: After Pluto, Makemake is the second-brightest object in the Kuiper belt.

name: Charon
desc: Half the size of Pluto, so big that the two orbit a point in space between them. Its red north pole is stained by gases escaping from Pluto’s atmosphere.
fact: Charon’s reddish polar cap is nicknamed Mordor Macula.

name: Phobos
desc: The larger, inner moon of Mars: a dark, potato-shaped rock, possibly a captured asteroid or debris from an ancient impact on Mars.
fact: Phobos orbits faster than Mars spins, so it rises in the west and sets in the east — twice a day. It is slowly spiralling inward.

name: Deimos
desc: Mars’s smaller, outer moon — smooth and dusty, with its craters half-buried in fine regolith.
fact: Seen from Mars, Deimos looks like a bright star and takes about two and a half days to cross the sky.

name: Io
desc: The most volcanically active world in the Solar System. Jupiter’s tides constantly squeeze Io, melting rock inside it to feed hundreds of volcanoes.
fact: Io’s volcanic plumes can rise hundreds of kilometres above its surface.

name: Europa
desc: A smooth shell of ice criss-crossed by long reddish cracks, floating on a global salty ocean that may hold twice as much water as Earth’s oceans.
fact: NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will investigate whether Europa’s hidden ocean could support life.

name: Ganymede
desc: The largest moon in the Solar System — bigger than the planet Mercury — and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field.
fact: ESA’s JUICE spacecraft is scheduled to enter orbit around Ganymede in 2034, the first spacecraft ever to orbit another planet’s moon.

name: Callisto
desc: One of the most heavily cratered surfaces known: an ancient, dark landscape that has barely changed in four billion years.
fact: Its biggest impact scar, Valhalla, is ringed by ridges spreading almost 4,000 km across.

name: Mimas
desc: A small icy moon dominated by Herschel crater, which is about a third as wide as Mimas itself.
fact: Thanks to Herschel crater, Mimas looks remarkably like the Death Star from Star Wars.

name: Enceladus
desc: The most reflective body in the Solar System. Jets of water vapour and ice spray from four “tiger stripe” cracks near its south pole.
fact: NASA’s Cassini flew straight through the plumes and found salty water and organic molecules from an underground ocean.

name: Tethys
desc: An icy moon with a giant crater, Odysseus, and a vast canyon, Ithaca Chasma, that wraps three-quarters of the way around it.
fact: Tethys is almost entirely water ice — it is barely denser than water.

name: Dione
desc: A cratered icy moon whose trailing side is streaked with bright cliffs of fractured ice.
fact: Dione may hide a liquid water ocean about 100 km beneath its crust.

name: Rhea
desc: Saturn’s second-largest moon: a cold, heavily cratered ball of water ice with a little rock.
fact: Rhea is one of the most heavily cratered moons around Saturn.

name: Titan
desc: Saturn’s largest moon is wrapped in a thick orange nitrogen haze, with rivers, lakes and seas of liquid methane on its surface.
fact: ESA’s Huygens probe landed on Titan in 2005. NASA’s Dragonfly rotorcraft is planned to launch in 2028 to fly across its dunes.

name: Iapetus
desc: A two-toned moon: its leading hemisphere is as dark as coal, the other as bright as snow. A tall ridge along its equator gives it a walnut shape.
fact: Cassini (the astronomer) noticed in 1671 that Iapetus could only be seen on one side of Saturn — because its dark half faces us on the other.

name: Miranda
desc: A patchwork world of grooves, ridges and cliffs. Its Verona Rupes may be the tallest cliff in the Solar System, about 20 km high. Voyager 2 photographed only its southern half in 1986 — the smooth grey area on the map is unexplored.
fact: A rock dropped from the top of Verona Rupes would fall for several minutes in Miranda’s weak gravity.

name: Ariel
desc: The brightest of Uranus’s large moons, crossed by long valleys that suggest a surprisingly active past. Voyager 2 photographed only its southern half in 1986 — the smooth grey area on the map is unexplored.
fact: Ariel’s surface is among the youngest of Uranus’s moons — fewer large craters survive there.

name: Umbriel
desc: The darkest of Uranus’s large moons, ancient and heavily cratered. Voyager 2 photographed only its southern half in 1986 — the smooth grey area on the map is unexplored.
fact: A mysterious bright ring, Wunda, sits on the floor of a crater near Umbriel’s equator.

name: Titania
desc: The largest moon of Uranus, split by enormous canyons that formed as its interior froze and expanded. Voyager 2 photographed only its southern half in 1986 — the smooth grey area on the map is unexplored.
fact: Titania and Oberon were the first moons of Uranus ever discovered — by the same astronomer who found Uranus.

name: Oberon
desc: The outermost of Uranus’s large moons: old, dark-floored craters and a mountain about 11 km tall. Voyager 2 photographed only its southern half in 1986 — the smooth grey area on the map is unexplored.
fact: Oberon spends part of its orbit outside Uranus’s magnetic field.

name: Triton
desc: Neptune’s giant moon orbits backwards, so it was probably a Kuiper belt world captured by Neptune. Voyager 2 saw nitrogen geysers erupting there in 1989. Only part of Triton has ever been photographed.
fact: Triton is slowly spiralling inward and may one day be torn apart to form a ring around Neptune.

name: Dysnomia
desc: Eris’s only known moon — a dark world, and the reason we know Eris’s mass: its orbit let astronomers weigh its parent.
fact: Eris spins exactly once per Dysnomia orbit, so the pair are tidally locked like Pluto and Charon.

name: Voyager 1
desc: Launched in 1977, it flew past Jupiter and Saturn (and Titan) before climbing out of the plane of the planets. In 2012 it became the first human-made object to enter interstellar space.
fact: In November 2026 Voyager 1 became one light-day from Earth — a radio message takes a full 24 hours to reach it.
status: Still talking to Earth from interstellar space

name: Voyager 2
desc: The only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus (1986) and Neptune (1989) — almost everything we know up close about those worlds and their moons comes from it.
fact: Neptune’s gravity bent Voyager 2 sharply “down”, below the plane of the planets, where it is still heading today.

name: New Horizons
desc: The fastest spacecraft ever launched from Earth. It gave us the first close-up views of Pluto and Charon in July 2015, then flew past the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth on New Year’s Day 2019.
fact: Its Arrokoth flyby, 43 AU from the Sun, is the most distant object ever explored up close.

name: Europa Clipper
desc: NASA’s largest planetary spacecraft, on its way to Jupiter’s moon Europa. It uses gravity assists from Mars (2025) and Earth (Dec 2026) to reach Jupiter in 2030.
fact: Its solar arrays span over 30 metres — wider than a basketball court is long.

name: Parker Solar Probe
desc: The closest any human-made object has come to the Sun: about 6.1 million km from its surface. At closest approach it moves at roughly 690,000 km/h — the fastest object ever built.
fact: Its heat shield faces temperatures near 1,400 °C while the instruments behind it stay close to room temperature. (Orbit orientation shown here is approximate.)
status: Diving through the Sun’s outer atmosphere every 88 days

name: James Webb Space Telescope
desc: The largest space telescope ever launched. It sits near the Sun–Earth L2 point, about 1.5 million km from Earth on the side away from the Sun, keeping its giant sunshield between it and the Sun, Earth and Moon.
fact: Its golden mirror is 6.5 metres across, made of 18 hexagonal segments. (Distance from Earth is exaggerated here so you can see it.)
status: Observing from 1.5 million km beyond Earth

name: Halley’s Comet
desc: The most famous periodic comet, seen and recorded for over 2,000 years. It orbits backwards compared with the planets.
fact: Its next visit to the inner Solar System is in mid-2061.

name: Comet Encke
desc: The comet with the shortest known period of any bright comet: it returns every 3.3 years and never travels beyond Jupiter’s orbit.
fact: Dust left behind by Encke causes the Taurid meteor showers every October–November.

name: 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko
desc: A rubber-duck-shaped comet about 4 km across. ESA’s Rosetta orbited it for two years and in 2014 its Philae lander made the first-ever landing on a comet.
fact: It returns to perihelion every 6.4 years.

name: Comet Hale–Bopp
desc: The “Great Comet of 1997”, visible to the naked eye for a record 18 months. Its nucleus is unusually large — around 60 km across.
fact: It will not return for roughly 2,500 years.
